metadata.note: The San Francisco and San Jose Railroad (1863-1870) and the Southern Pacific's Peninsula Commute (1870-June 30 1992), the predecessors of Caltrain (see caltrain.geojson from July 1 1992). The SF&SJ opened from Valencia Street in San Francisco to Mayfield in October 1863 and reached San Jose's Market Street depot on January 16 1864. Until the Bayshore Cutoff opened on December 8 1907 the line ran inland through the Bernal Cut and west of San Bruno Mountain via Colma; that route kept a passenger service as the Ocean View Branch until November 1928. SP's Townsend Street terminal replaced Valencia Street in August 1874. SP subsidiary operation continued under Caltrans from 1980 and under the CalTrain name from 1985 until the Peninsula Corridor Joint Powers Board took over on July 1 1992 with Amtrak as contract operator.

metadata.caltrain_audit_2026_10_14: Rebuilt: the single SF-SJ shape (drawn from 1863 on the post-1907 Bayshore Cutoff route, and to San Jose before the line reached it) was split into the 1863 Mayfield section, the 1864 San Jose section, the pre-1907 route via Colma (OHM) and the Bayshore Cutoff; SF&SJ given its own colour (it was a separate company until 1870, Rule 4); SP's years extended from 1985 to June 30 1992, when SP stopped running the trains; the Ocean View Branch's post-1907 passenger service added through 1928.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.

segments.note: First section of the SF&SJ, from a Valencia Street terminal in San Francisco through the Bernal Cut, west of San Bruno Mountain via Colma, to San Bruno and down the Peninsula to Mayfield (today's California Avenue, Palo Alto). Opened October 1863. SOURCE CONFLICT on the day: Wikipedia's SF&SJ article gives an excursion on October 17 and daily service from October 18; its Ocean View Branch article gives October 23. SOURCE CONFLICT on the San Francisco terminal: Caltrain says 18th and Valencia; Wikipedia variously gives 16th and Valencia, 18th and Valencia, and a Valencia Street station near 25th. Drawn from 18th and Valencia. Ends 1870, when the SF&SJ was consolidated into the Southern Pacific (Wikipedia also says the SP group acquired control in March 1868). headway_min is an estimate.
sources: Segment-level: opening month, route and 1870 consolidation checked against the sources below; headway_min is an estimate, not from a timetable.

segments.note: Wikipedia's Ocean View Branch article says that by around 1866 trains again ran up Valencia Street to a new depot at Market Street. The 1864 extension down Harrison Street to a depot on Brannan Street (opened February 14 1864) is not drawn: the same article says most passenger trains soon reverted to Valencia Street, and when Brannan stopped seeing passenger trains is not sourced. headway_min is an estimate.

segments.note: SP inherited the SF&SJ's San Francisco terminal on Valencia Street at Market. Ends 1874, when SP's Townsend Street terminal opened (August 17 1874) and became the San Francisco terminal; whether any passenger trains still ran up Valencia Street to Market afterwards is not sourced. headway_min is an estimate.
sources: Segment-level: the 1874 Townsend Street opening is from the sources below; the end of Valencia Street passenger service is not sourced. headway_min is an estimate.

properties.line: Southern Pacific: Townsend Street – Valencia Street (Harrison St)
properties.geometry_quality: OpenHistoricalMap ways (CC0, geometry only; OHM's own dates were not used) traced from the 1892-1915 USGS San Mateo sheets and the 1912 SF commercial atlas (ways 200016941, 199446972, 199446971), 3.0 mi from the Townsend Street depot to the Bernal Cut junction. OHM dates this route 1891; the 1874 start comes from the written sources, so the drawn alignment may be a later one through the city.

segments.note: From August 17 1874 Peninsula trains ran from SP's Townsend Street terminal (between 3rd and 4th; a new 3rd and Townsend station opened April 15 1889) out along Harrison Street to the Bernal Cut. This was the main line until the Bayshore Cutoff opened December 8 1907. headway_min is an estimate.
sources: Segment-level: the 1874, 1889 and 1907 dates are from the sources below; headway_min is an estimate.

segments.note: After the cutoff, the old route became the Ocean View Branch, with 3-4 daily round trips by 1913 and one from June 1919 until passenger service was suspended in November 1928. NOT SOURCED: which city approach those trains used after 1907. They are drawn here on the Harrison Street line because that is the track they had; they may instead have reached the branch from the Bayshore main line. headway_min is derived from the 1913 count and overstates 1919-1928.
sources: Segment-level: round-trip counts and the 1928 suspension are from the Ocean View Branch article; the post-1907 approach through the city is NOT SOURCED.

segments.note: The original SF&SJ main line through the Bernal Cut and west of San Bruno Mountain via Ocean View, Daly City and Colma to San Bruno, run by the Southern Pacific from 1870 until the Bayshore Cutoff opened December 8 1907. headway_min is an estimate.
sources: Segment-level: route and the 1907 cutoff date are from the sources below; headway_min is an estimate.

segments.note: As the Ocean View Branch it kept a passenger service after 1907: 3-4 daily round trips by 1913, cut to one in June 1919. Passenger service was suspended in November 1928 while the Bernal Cut was widened for San Jose Avenue, and the suspension became permanent in March 1930. SOURCE CONFLICT: Wikipedia's Peninsula Commute article says the branch was freight-only south of Daly City after 1907; the Ocean View Branch article, which cites the timetables, is followed. Freight continued until 1942 north of Ocean Avenue and 1978 Daly City - South San Francisco. headway_min is derived from the 1913 count and overstates 1919-1928.
sources: Segment-level: passenger dates and counts checked against the Ocean View Branch article; the conflict with the Peninsula Commute article is recorded in the note.

properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OpenStreetMap 2026-10-14 along ways named 'Caltrain Peninsula Subdivision' (Dijkstra over railway=rail, mainline-preferred, no bridged gaps). 10.9 mi from 4th and King to San Bruno. LATER ALIGNMENT THAN SOME OF THE ERA DRAWN: (1) the San Francisco terminal was 3rd and Townsend until 1975, about 300 m north-east of the 4th and King end drawn here; (2) the line at Brisbane was realigned for the Bayshore Freeway around 1956 (OpenHistoricalMap), so 1907-1956 is drawn on the later track.

segments.note: The Bayshore Cutoff opened December 8 1907, carrying Peninsula trains along the bay east of San Bruno Mountain through five tunnels. Wikipedia says there were more than two dozen daily round trips by 1913 (about 48 trains, so about 30 minutes as a day average). Ridership peaked in World War II; SOURCE CONFLICT on counts: Wikipedia gives 26 trains a day in the war and 22 in 1970, both hard to square with 44 in 1977. headway_min is the 1913 figure carried forward and is an estimate for later years.
sources: Segment-level: 1907 opening and 1913 count checked against the sources below; headway after 1913 is an estimate.

segments.note: In May 1977, when SP petitioned to discontinue the commute, it ran 44 trains a day. The CPUC denied the petition in April 1978.
sources: Segment-level: 44 trains a day in 1977, from the Peninsula Commute article.

segments.note: From July 1 1980 the service was subsidised by Caltrans, with SP still running the trains under contract; it was branded CalTrain from 1985. Weekday trains rose from 44 to 54 by June 1992; headway_min uses 50 as the era average. SP's operation ended June 30 1992 (see caltrain.geojson from July 1 1992).
sources: Segment-level: 1980, 1985 and June 30 1992 dates and the 54-train count are from the sources below; the headway is an average across the era.
